stories.headline: Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed Wins Landslide Election Amid Growing Conflict Fears
stories.summary:
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's Prosperity Party won a decisive parliamentary majority, claiming 438 of 501 contested seats in Sunday's general election. Abiy is expected to be sworn in for another term in October, extending his hold on power in Africa's second most-populous nation.

The vote was shadowed by serious concerns about legitimacy and stability. The Tigray region, home to six million people and 38 constituencies, was entirely excluded from the election. Armed militias in the Amhara and Oromia regions caused 143 polling stations to fail to open on election day, and both the Fano militias and the Oromo Liberation Army rejected the results.

Security analysts warn Ethiopia may be heading back to large-scale conflict. Relations between Addis Ababa and Eritrea have sharply deteriorated since the 2022 Tigray ceasefire, with Eritrea now allied with Tigrayan forces — a realignment that could fuel renewed fighting. Ethiopia has also been accused of backing the RSF faction in Sudan's civil war, which it denies.

Abiy, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 for reconciliation with Eritrea, now faces a fractured internal security picture. His supporters argue he will continue economic gains, while critics say the election's narrow participation and ongoing insurgencies undermine any claim to a democratic mandate.

stories.headline: Brexit at Ten: UK Economy Smaller Than Pre-Vote Projections, Divisions Remain
stories.summary:
June 23 marks ten years since the United Kingdom voted 52%-48% to leave the European Union, a referendum that triggered the most significant restructuring of the British economy and political identity since World War II. The formal departure took nearly five more years to complete.

Economic assessments of Brexit's impact are broadly negative among mainstream analysts. Experts estimate the UK economy is between 4% and 8% smaller than it would have been had the country remained in the EU, translating to reduced living standards and lower public revenue. Non-tariff barriers including customs paperwork, border certifications, and visa restrictions have complicated trade with the EU, which remains the UK's largest trading partner. Major trade deals promised by Brexit supporters, including one with the United States, have not materialized.

Supporters of Brexit argue the economic costs were an expected short-term disruption and that the long-term gains — greater control over immigration, regulatory independence, and domestic policy levers — cannot yet be fully judged. They contend the UK's struggles are also attributable to the COVID-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and other global disruptions that would have affected the country regardless of its EU membership status.

The anniversary arrives as Britain faces fresh political uncertainty, with Prime Minister Keir Starmer reportedly preparing to set an exit timetable. Public debate over whether to pursue closer ties with the EU has intensified, though a formal rejoining remains politically distant.

stories.headline: Trump Calls for Military Intervention in Chicago After Weekend Shootings Leave 7 Dead, 38 Injured
stories.summary:
A series of shootings across Chicago between Friday evening and Sunday left at least seven people dead and 38 injured, prompting President Donald Trump to renew calls for federal military intervention in the city. In a Sunday morning Truth Social post, Trump challenged Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker — a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate — to request federal assistance, claiming he could make Chicago safe within a month or a year.

Police said preliminary data shows at least two dozen shooting incidents since 5 p.m. Friday, including a mass shooting on Juneteenth in which an SUV pulled up to a crowd and two occupants opened fire, wounding 12 people ranging in age from 17 to 47. Those killed include a 21-year-old, an 18-year-old, and a 50-year-old. The holiday shootings drew particular attention given that former President Barack Obama's presidential center had opened on Chicago's South Side earlier that day.

Mayor Brandon Johnson condemned the violence as shattering what should have been a night of community celebration. Governor Pritzker's office did not respond to Trump's challenge. Chicago Police Department data shows a slight uptick in shooting incidents compared to the same period last year, though overall violent crime rates in the city have broadly declined over recent years.

The episode renews a long-running political confrontation between the Trump administration and Democratic-led cities over federal law enforcement authority. Trump has previously deployed National Guard troops on crime-fighting missions in New Orleans, Washington, D.C., and Memphis — moves Democrats have characterized as unconstitutional overreach while Republicans argue they are necessary to restore order.

stories.headline: Serena Williams Granted Wimbledon Singles Wild Card for First Grand Slam Singles Return Since 2022
stories.summary:
Serena Williams will compete in the singles draw at Wimbledon 2026 after receiving a wild-card entry from tournament organizers, the All England Club announced Sunday. The appearance will mark the 44-year-old's first singles competition at a Grand Slam since the 2022 U.S. Open, where she retired from professional tennis.

Williams had already been awarded a wild card for the ladies' doubles draw alongside her sister Venus. Her singles comeback follows a recent return to doubles competition: she and Victoria Mboko won their opening match at Queen's Club before Mboko's injury cut short the run, and she subsequently partnered Karolina Muchova at the Berlin Open, where they lost in the first round.

A 23-time Grand Slam singles champion, Williams is one title shy of Margaret Court's all-time record of 24. Wimbledon 2026 begins next Monday.

stories.headline: European Heat Wave Prompts State of Emergency Measures in France; Multiple Drownings Reported
stories.summary:
A severe heat wave gripped parts of Europe on Sunday, with about a third of France placed under a "red alert" as temperatures reached 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in some areas. French authorities canceled trains, concerts, and outdoor sports events, and banned public drinking in red-alert zones, while the government mobilized emergency services and military forces for heightened wildfire readiness.

Four children drowned in France on Saturday as people sought relief in rivers and lakes, and multiple additional drowning deaths were reported across the continent. France's annual Music Day celebration, which draws thousands of concerts across the country, was partially canceled, and the Eiffel Tower set up misting stations for crowds. Tourists in Rome sheltered in fountains while Spain's Basque Country also canceled sports and cultural events.

The World Health Organization's Europe office reported earlier this month that more than 200,000 people across Europe died from heat-related causes over the past four years, with most fatalities considered preventable. A rapid attribution study found that human-caused climate change was responsible for approximately 1,500 deaths in an unusually early European heat wave in May, and U.N. climate projections indicate the next five years are likely to break further heat records.

French authorities expressed particular concern for elderly and homeless people, recalling the catastrophic 2003 heat wave that killed approximately 15,000 older people in France. The forecast for Monday was expected to be even hotter than Sunday, and nuclear plant water supply surveillance was tightened as a precaution.

stories.headline: Xi Jinping Completes First North Korea Visit in Seven Years as China Reasserts Influence
stories.summary:
Chinese President Xi Jinping wrapped up a two-day state visit to Pyongyang, his first official trip to North Korea since 2019, signaling Beijing's effort to reassert influence over a strategically vital but increasingly unpredictable partner. The visit comes amid heightened tensions on the Korean Peninsula and broader shifts in the global order driven by the U.S.-Iran conflict and evolving U.S.-China competition.

Beijing views its relationship with Pyongyang as a key strategic buffer and has sought to manage North Korea's alignment as Pyongyang has deepened military cooperation with Russia during the Ukraine war. The visit represents an attempt by Xi to stabilize and reinforce that relationship at a moment when China faces pressure on multiple fronts, including trade tensions with the United States and scrutiny over its regional ambitions.

Details of specific agreements or outcomes from the summit were not immediately disclosed. The visit received a ceremonial welcome from North Korean officials and is expected to address economic ties, denuclearization posture, and bilateral security arrangements, though Pyongyang's nuclear program remains a persistent source of tension between its public positions and international demands.

The timing of the visit, concurrent with the U.S.-Iran nuclear talks in Switzerland, underscores the degree to which global powers are recalibrating relationships amid a period of significant geopolitical flux. Analysts note that China's renewed engagement with North Korea could complicate any broader U.S. diplomatic initiatives in Asia.

stories.headline: Obama Says U.S. Is 'Worse Off' After Iran War as Trump Pushes Back
stories.summary:
Former President Barack Obama said in a Friday interview that the United States is in a worse position following its military conflict with Iran than it was before the war began. 'We've now fought a war, spent billions and billions of dollars, put enormous strain on our military. A lot of people have died. And it feels like we're back where we were before we started the war, except maybe a little bit worse off,' Obama told NBC's TODAY program. He expressed relief at the reported ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah but argued the original rationale for military action — preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons — had not been achieved.

Obama specifically pointed to the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, which his administration negotiated, as a framework that had constrained Iran's nuclear program before Trump withdrew from it during his first term in 2018. He argued that withdrawal caused Iran to expand its nuclear capacity, ultimately contributing to the conditions that led to the conflict. Obama's remarks come as the U.S.-Iran Memorandum of Understanding remains in a fragile state, with continued Israel-Hezbollah fighting threatening to unravel the agreement's 60-day negotiating window.

President Trump responded Saturday on Truth Social, dismissing critics as 'Dumocrats' and arguing that Iran had been 'defeated militarily, with no Navy or Air Force.' The White House and Trump allies maintain that Operation Epic Fury significantly degraded Iran's military capabilities and brought Tehran to the negotiating table. However, Trump separately drew scrutiny this week after suggesting at the G7 that Iran retaining some ballistic missiles may be acceptable — a position that appears to contradict earlier administration statements that destroying Iran's missile arsenal was a central war objective.

The exchange underscores a deepening partisan divide over how to assess the conflict's outcome. Critics, including Obama, argue the war achieved little beyond destruction while leaving Iran's nuclear ambitions unresolved. Supporters contend military pressure forced concessions that diplomacy alone could not. The debate is expected to intensify ahead of November midterm elections, with Republicans defending the operation and Democrats framing it as a costly strategic miscalculation.

stories.headline: Ukraine Cuts Fuel Supplies in Crimea After Drone Strike on Oil Depot; Russia Shoots Down 239 Drones
stories.summary:
Russian-backed authorities in occupied Crimea suspended all public fuel sales Sunday after Ukrainian drone strikes on an oil depot in Kerch killed four people and injured 28, causing critical shortages across the peninsula. Governor Sergey Aksyonov announced that petrol stations would serve only government agencies essential to Crimea's 'functioning and security,' marking the most severe fuel restriction on the occupied territory since Russia's 2014 annexation. Aksyonov said further decisions on the fuel market situation would be announced later.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the Kerch strike as a 'just response to Russia's brutal attacks' and said Kyiv had also struck a logistics facility for oil transportation in Russia's adjacent Krasnodar region, killing one person on a passenger ferry. Military logistics facilities and radar systems were additionally targeted overnight. Russia's defense ministry said its forces shot down 239 Ukrainian drones in the exchange, highlighting the scale of the overnight campaign.

Zelensky reported at least seven Ukrainians killed in Russian attacks over the weekend, with children among more than 30 injured. The strikes reflect Kyiv's dual strategy of choking Moscow's fuel export revenue while maximizing disruption to Russian-occupied civilian life in hopes of pressuring President Vladimir Putin toward negotiations. Putin has shown no signs of readiness to engage, having rebuffed Zelensky's request for direct talks earlier this month.

Crimea serves as a strategically vital launch pad for Russian strikes into Ukraine and as a major summer holiday destination for Russians, some of whom have reported difficulty finding petrol to return home. The intensity of cross-border attacks has escalated significantly in recent months as ceasefire efforts remain stalled more than four years into Russia's full-scale invasion.

stories.headline: Israeli Strike Kills Al Jazeera Cameraman in Gaza; IDF Says He Was a Hamas Operative
stories.summary:
An Israeli airstrike on a home in the Bureij refugee camp in central Gaza on Saturday killed Al Jazeera cameraman Ahmed Wishah along with two other people, according to a local hospital and Hamas-run civil defense officials. Al Jazeera condemned the killing as 'a heinous crime' and 'a continued systematic policy of targeting journalists,' saying it constitutes a 'flagrant violation of all international laws and norms.' Wishah's brother Mohamed, also an Al Jazeera correspondent, was killed in a separate Israeli strike in April.

The Israel Defense Forces said Wishah was 'a terrorist in Hamas' military wing who served as a sniper operative' who had in recent months advanced sniper attack plans against Israeli troops. The IDF also accused the two others killed in the strike of Hamas affiliation, without providing additional evidence. A separate overnight strike in Gaza City's Sabra neighborhood killed four family members, including two children and two women, according to civil defense, medics, and relatives. Survivors denied any connection to Hamas.

Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the United Nations regards as reliable, said the Israeli military has killed 1,007 people since a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas took effect last October. Both Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire since it was established. UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher told the Security Council this week that the share of Gaza households going to bed hungry had dropped from 92% to 36% since the ceasefire, as more aid trucks entered the territory.

Despite the improvement in aid access, Fletcher said 70% of Gaza's population still lacks proper shelter, sanitation conditions are deteriorating, and essential services remain 'on the brink.' The killing of the second Al Jazeera journalist in two months is expected to intensify international debate over Israel's targeting practices and press freedom in the conflict zone.

stories.headline: Update: Vance Arrives in Switzerland as Iran Closes Strait of Hormuz, Complicating Peace Talks
stories.summary:
Vice President JD Vance arrived in Switzerland on Sunday to join special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner for technical-level negotiations with Iran, aimed at building on the recently signed memorandum of understanding to end hostilities. The talks, originally scheduled for Friday, were delayed after Iran's armed forces announced they were closing the Strait of Hormuz — just three days after it had reopened — citing continued Israeli strikes on Hezbollah in Lebanon as violations of the interim ceasefire deal.

Iran's top military command said the waterway closure was a direct response to Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon that it said violated the U.S.-Iran agreement. Vance, speaking on Fox News before departing, said he had seen no evidence that Iran had actually blocked the strait, and the U.S. disputed Iran's claim outright. Pakistan, one of the key mediators, confirmed that talks would proceed in Switzerland on Sunday, with Islamabad sending its prime minister and military chief to participate.

President Trump, responding on Truth Social, threatened to impose tolls on the Strait of Hormuz if a permanent deal is not completed within 60 days. Trump also suggested that Iran retaining some missile capability may be acceptable, striking a notably different tone from the administration's earlier justifications for military action. He separately lashed out at critics of the MOU, calling Democratic opponents "Radical Left fools."

The episode represents the first significant crisis to emerge since the MOU was signed, and it underscores the fragility of the peace framework. Republicans are divided on the deal, with some praising progress on the nuclear file while others warn the agreement grants Tehran billions in economic relief without enforceable inspection mechanisms. Democrats have largely argued the war produced no concrete gains while inflicting economic pain on American consumers through energy price disruptions.

stories.headline: Update: Keir Starmer Expected to Resign as UK Prime Minister, Set Exit Timetable
stories.summary:
Britain's Observer newspaper reported that Prime Minister Keir Starmer is expected to announce his resignation on Monday and set out a timetable for an orderly departure, a development that would end his tenure less than two years after Labour's landslide election victory. A government source pushed back, telling Reuters that Starmer remained focused on governing, but a cabinet ally separately acknowledged the prime minister was weighing "political realities."

UK Business Secretary Peter Kyle said publicly that Starmer is reflecting on those realities, a notably candid admission that added weight to the resignation reports. The political pressure on Starmer has intensified following Andy Burnham's return to Parliament after winning a by-election, positioning the Greater Manchester mayor as a prominent leadership challenger.

Starmer's premiership has been battered by persistently low approval ratings, internal party tensions, and difficult economic conditions. His government faced criticism from both the left — over perceived moderation on key Labour policy commitments — and from centrists concerned about electoral vulnerabilities heading toward the next general election.

If confirmed, Starmer's departure would trigger a Labour leadership contest at a critical moment for British politics, with the opposition Conservatives still rebuilding and Reform UK gaining ground in polls. The transition would mark a significant moment for the UK's governing coalition and its relationships with European partners and the United States.

stories.headline: Update: Trump-Meloni Feud Deepens as Italy Cancels U.S. Diplomatic Visit
stories.summary:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni publicly told President Trump to "focus on your own popularity" in a pointed Instagram statement on Saturday, escalating a public dispute that has strained one of Trump's previously closest European relationships. Trump had renewed his attack on Meloni, accusing her of requesting a photo with him "over and over" at the G7 summit in France and claiming she had caused a "great logistical inconvenience" by denying U.S. forces access to Italian air facilities during military operations against Iran.

Meloni rejected both claims, saying Italian base access is governed by existing agreements "that cannot be violated as long as I am prime minister," and that Trump's attacks were "constant, unprovoked" and "senseless." She noted pointedly that being Trump's friend had not helped her domestic approval ratings. Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani subsequently cancelled a planned visit to Washington scheduled for early next week.

The confrontation has drawn support for Meloni from across Italy's political spectrum, including from opposition parties, and reflects growing European frustration with Trump's conduct toward allied governments. Italy was the sole European nation to send its leader to Trump's inauguration in January 2025, and Meloni had cultivated a close personal relationship with the American president built on shared right-nationalist political affinities.

The rift traces in part to Italy's refusal to allow U.S. use of its bases during the Iran war, which Trump and Italian officials characterize very differently. The public exchange marks a significant deterioration in transatlantic relations at a moment when the U.S. is simultaneously negotiating a fragile peace framework in the Middle East and pressing NATO allies on defense spending commitments.

stories.headline: Colombia Presidential Runoff Pits Leftist Negotiator Against Trump-Backed Security Hardliner
stories.summary:
Colombians head to the polls Sunday in a high-stakes presidential runoff that presents starkly contrasting visions for addressing the country's escalating internal conflict. Left-wing senator Iván Cepeda, the architect of outgoing President Gustavo Petro's "total peace" strategy of negotiating with armed groups, faces conservative businessman Abelardo de la Espriella — known as El Tigre — who has promised mass incarceration, military crackdowns, and an end to all negotiations with cartels and guerrilla factions.

The election comes as illegal armed groups, including FARC dissident factions, the ELN, and the Clan del Golfo, have roughly doubled their membership over the last five years, driving a reported 300 percent increase in forced displacement between 2024 and 2025. Tens of thousands of Colombians have been displaced by renewed fighting near the Venezuelan border, and the campaign itself was marked by the assassination of a presidential candidate, along with widespread homicides, kidnappings, and bombings.

De la Espriella, who holds U.S. citizenship and has received Donald Trump's endorsement, has promised ten mega-prisons and a military offensive against armed groups, saying any criminal who does not surrender "will be taken down." Critics of Cepeda's approach argue that the Petro government's negotiation strategy allowed armed groups to exploit ceasefire periods to expand territorial control; supporters say it prevented greater bloodshed.

The outcome will have significant implications for U.S.-Colombia relations, drug trafficking interdiction cooperation, and the future of the 2016 peace agreement that disarmed thousands of FARC fighters. Colombia remains the world's leading cocaine producer, and the stability of its government is closely watched across Latin America and in Washington.
